title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: The streets were still empty. Levin walked over to the Shtcherbatskys' house. The front doors were closed and everything was asleep. He walked back, returned to his room, and asked for coffee. The day servant, not Yegor this time, brought it to him. Levin would have struck up a conversation with him, but a bell rang for the servant and he went out. Levin tried to drink coffee and put a roll in his mouth, but his mouth simply had no idea what to do with the roll. He rejected the roll, put on his coat, and went out for another walk. It was nine o'clock when he reached the Shtcherbatskys' steps a second time. In the house they were only just up, and the cook came out to go to market. He had at least two more hours to get through.

Through all that night and morning Levin had been living completely unconsciously, feeling lifted out of the conditions of material life altogether. He had eaten nothing for a whole day, had not slept for two nights, had spent several hours half-undressed in the freezing air — and felt not merely fresher and stronger than ever, but altogether independent of his body; he moved without any muscular effort and felt as though he could do anything. He was convinced that he could fly up into the air or lift the corner of the house if need be. He spent the remainder of the time on the street, constantly looking at his watch and gazing about him.

And what he saw then he never saw again afterwards. The children, especially, going to school, the bluish doves flying down from the rooftops to the pavement, and the little loaves dusted with flour, pushed out by an unseen hand — these things touched him. Those loaves, those doves, and those two boys were not creatures of this earth. It all happened at the same instant: a boy ran toward a dove and looked up at Levin, smiling; the dove, with a whir of her wings, darted away, flashing in the sun amid grains of snow that quivered in the air, while from a little window came the smell of fresh-baked bread, and the loaves were put out. All this together was so extraordinarily lovely that Levin laughed and cried with delight. Taking a long roundabout route through Gazetny Place and Kislovka, he went back to the hotel, and setting his watch in front of him, sat down to wait for twelve o'clock. In the next room they were talking about some kind of machines and about swindling, and coughing their morning coughs. They did not realize that the hand was near twelve. The hand reached it. Levin walked out onto the steps. The sledge drivers clearly knew all about it. They crowded round Levin with happy faces, quarreling among themselves and offering their services. Trying not to offend the others, and promising to drive with them too, Levin took one and told him to drive to the Shtcherbatskys'. The sledge driver was splendid, with a white shirt collar sticking out over his overcoat and into his strong, full-blooded red neck. The sledge was high and comfortable, the sort Levin never drove in afterwards, and the horse was a good one, and tried to gallop yet didn't seem to be moving. The driver knew the Shtcherbatskys' house, and drew up at the entrance with a flourish of his arm and a "Wo!" expressly indicating his respect for his fare. The Shtcherbatskys' hall-porter certainly knew all about it. That was plain from the smile in his eyes and the way he said:
"It's been a long time since you came to see us, Konstantin Dmitrievitch!"
Not only did he know all about it — he was unmistakably delighted and trying to hide his joy. Looking into his kindly old eyes, Levin realized something new in his happiness.
"Are they up?"
"Pray walk in! Leave it here," he said, smiling, as Levin would have come back for his hat. That meant something.
"Whom shall I announce to her honor?" asked the footman.
The footman, though a young man and one of the new school of footmen, a dandy, was a very kind-hearted, decent fellow, and he too knew all about it.
"The princess ... the prince ... the young princess...." said Levin.

The first person he saw was Mademoiselle Linon. She walked across the room, and her ringlets and her face were beaming. He had barely spoken to her when he suddenly heard the rustle of a skirt at the door, and Mademoiselle Linon vanished from Levin's sight, and a joyful terror came over him at the nearness of his happiness. Mademoiselle Linon was in a great hurry, and leaving him, went out by the other door. The moment she was gone, swift, swift light steps sounded on the parquet, and his bliss, his life, himself — what was best in himself, what he had so long sought and longed for — was quickly, so quickly approaching him. She did not walk so much as float, by some invisible force, toward him. He saw nothing but her clear, truthful eyes, frightened by the same bliss of love that flooded his own heart. Those eyes shone nearer and nearer, blinding him with their light of love. She stopped close to him, touching him. Her hands rose and dropped onto his shoulders.
She had done all she could — she had run up to him and given herself over entirely, shy and happy. He put his arms around her and pressed his lips to her mouth that sought his kiss.
She, too, had not slept all night, and had been expecting him all morning.

Her mother and father had agreed without demur and were happy in her happiness. She had been waiting for him. She had wanted to be the first to tell him her happiness and his. She had got herself ready to see him alone, and had been delighted at the prospect, and shy and ashamed, and did not know herself what she was doing. She had heard his steps and voice and had waited at the door for Mademoiselle Linon to leave. Mademoiselle Linon had gone. Without thinking, without asking herself how or what, she had gone up to him and done what she did.

"Let's go to mamma!" she said, taking him by the hand. For a long while he could say nothing — not so much because he was afraid of desecrating the loftiness of his emotion with a word, as because every time he tried to speak, instead of words he felt tears of happiness welling up. He took her hand and kissed it.
"Can it really be true?" he said at last in a choked voice. "I cannot believe you love me, my dear!"
She smiled at that "dear," and at the shyness with which he glanced at her.
"Yes!" she said meaningfully, deliberately. "I am so happy!"

Not letting go of his hands, she went into the drawing room. The princess, seeing them, breathed quickly and immediately began to cry, and then immediately began to laugh, and with a vigorous step Levin had not expected from her, ran up to him and, hugging his head, kissed him, wetting his cheeks with her tears.
"So it's all settled! I am glad. Love her. I am glad.... Kitty!"
"You haven't been long settling things," said the old prince, trying to seem unmoved; but Levin noticed that his eyes were wet when he turned to him.
"I have long, always wanted this!" said the prince, taking Levin by the arm and drawing him toward himself. "Even when this little featherhead fancied...."
"Papa!" shrieked Kitty, and shut his mouth with her hands.
"All right, I won't!" he said. "I'm very, very ... plea... Oh, what a fool I am...."
He embraced Kitty, kissed her face, her hand, her face again, and made the sign of the cross over her.
And a new feeling of love came over Levin for this man, until then so little known to him, when he saw how slowly and tenderly Kitty kissed his muscular hand.
